result: The insula plays a fundamental role in adaptive human behaviors, cognitive control, and awareness, but its electrophysiological dynamics and hierarchical organization are poorly understood.
evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C15 establish the insula's functional importance through citations to prior literature, while C2 and C29 identify the knowledge gap. These claims provide appropriate context and motivation for the study, supported by established literature.

result: Theta (~6-9 Hz) and beta (~15-32 Hz) oscillations are widespread and spontaneously present in the insula, organized largely along the anterior-posterior axis, with no 9-15 Hz oscillations detected.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4 state the main finding, while C46-C50 provide quantitative support showing ~80-99% of electrodes exhibited these oscillations across hemispheres. The absence of 9-15 Hz oscillations (C50) is explicitly shown in Figure 1. The data directly support these claims.

result: Both left and right insula showed anterior-to-posterior decreasing gradients for beta oscillation power, with higher power anteriorly.
evaluation: Claims C59 and C62 provide statistical evidence (t[84]=3.07, p<0.01 for left; t[58]=2.97, p<0.01 for right) from LME models, with C63 summarizing the bilateral finding. The statistical tests are appropriate and account for inter-subject variability.

result: The left insula showed a posterior-to-anterior decreasing frequency gradient and an anterior-to-posterior decreasing power gradient in the theta frequency band, with no gradients along the superior-inferior axis.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 provide statistical support (t[74]=-4.09, p<0.001 for frequency; t[84]=2.52, p<0.05 for power) from LME models. Claims C53-C54 report non-significant SI gradients (p>0.05). The statistical approach is appropriate and accounts for subject variability.

result: In the right insula, theta frequencies showed no AP or SI gradients, but theta power showed a marginally significant AP gradient (p=0.053) and a significant SI gradient with higher amplitudes superiorly (p<0.01).
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 provide statistical evidence from LME models. The marginally significant AP gradient (C57) and significant SI gradient (C58) are appropriately reported with exact p-values. The hemispheric asymmetry in theta organization is well-documented.

result: Beta frequency showed no hierarchical organization along AP or SI axes in either hemisphere.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C64-C65 report non-significant effects (all p>0.05) from LME models for both hemispheres. The statistical tests are appropriate and the negative findings are clearly reported.

result: Traveling waves were detected in theta and beta bands in the human insula for the first time, present in ~35% of timepoints across 93% of oscillation clusters, with median propagation speed of ~0.7 m/s.
evaluation: Claims C67-C73 provide detailed quantitative findings about cluster identification and traveling wave prevalence. C74 reports propagation speed consistent with prior cortical surface studies (C75). The novel circular-linear regression method and permutation testing provide rigorous statistical support. This represents a major novel finding.

result: The strength of traveling waves was positively correlated with oscillation amplitude in ~71% of clusters, with amplitude increases preceding wave-strength increases by 8 ms (theta) and 4 ms (beta), suggesting a causal role.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77 report significant correlations in 71% of clusters with appropriate statistical testing. However, the causal interpretation (C79) based on temporal delays (C78) of 4-8 ms is speculative. Cross-correlation analysis shows temporal precedence but cannot establish causation without additional experimental manipulation or modeling.

result: Theta and beta traveling waves were uncoupled in terms of phase, amplitude, and wave-strength, operating independently across the insula.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 provide statistical evidence showing no correlations (p>0.05) between theta and beta traveling wave properties for all but two clusters. The permutation testing approach is appropriate. The independence interpretation (C82) is well-supported by the data.

result: The study used resting-state iEEG recordings from 10 epilepsy patients with 239 electrodes in the insula, with ~97% of contacts in gray matter and the insula not being the seizure onset zone.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31, C83, C86-C97 provide comprehensive methodological details about participants, recording parameters, and electrode localization. The exclusion of seizure onset zones (C89) and high proportion of gray matter contacts (C97) strengthen data quality. Methods are clearly described.

result: Based on prior MEG studies showing brain-wide posterior-to-anterior frequency gradients and anterior-to-posterior power gradients, the authors hypothesized similar gradients in the insula.
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 cite prior MEG work (Mahjoory et al., 2020) establishing the precedent, and C35 states the hypothesis. The hypothesis is appropriately grounded in prior literature, though the actual findings showed hemispheric asymmetry not fully predicted by the hypothesis.

result: Computational modeling shows traveling waves can emerge from spatially varying frequency gradients in weakly coupled oscillators.
evaluation: Claim C66 cites Ermentrout and Kopell (1984) for this theoretical foundation. This provides appropriate theoretical motivation for investigating traveling waves given the observed frequency gradients.

result: Spontaneous gradients and traveling waves in the insula suggest a fundamental new principle for linking insula processing to widespread cortical areas.
evaluation: Claim C85 is a speculative interpretation of the findings. While the observed gradients and traveling waves are well-supported, the claim that this represents a 'fundamental new principle' for inter-regional communication is not directly tested and remains hypothetical. Additional experiments would be needed to establish this mechanistic link.
